title: Children’s understanding of cancer: the role of age and direct illness experience
abstract: Abstract Objective This study examined how age and direct cancer experience influence children’s understanding of cancer. Methods Participants were 104 children aged 6–14 years, including 52 pediatric oncology patients and 52 healthy peers. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted to assess children’s understanding across four domains: cancer identification, perceived severity, prognosis, and causal attribution. Data were analyzed using a mixed-methods approach. Qualitative responses were coded using content analysis with inductively derived categories, transformed into categorical variables for quantitative analyses. Logistic and ordinal regression analyses examined associations with age and illness experience, and multiple correspondence analysis explored co-occurring response profiles. Results Age was the primary predictor of understanding. Older children demonstrated more accurate identification of cancer [odds ratio (OR) = 1.05, 95% confidence interval (CI) (1.02–1.08), p = .002) and endorsed mechanistic explanations involving external (OR = 1.03, 95% CI [1.00–1.06], p = .041) or uncontrollable causes (OR = 1.03, 95% CI [1.00–1.06], p = .053). Younger children relied on intuitive explanations, including anecdotal and contagion-based reasoning, regardless of illness experience. Compared to healthy peers, children with cancer were less likely to perceive the illness as life-threatening (OR = 0.04, 95% CI [0.004–0.312], p = .003) and more likely to consider it curable. However, direct experience did not enhance accuracy, and did not substantially alter explanatory frameworks. Conclusions Findings highlight the central role of development in shaping children’s understanding of cancer. Younger children may be particularly vulnerable to misconceptions, emphasizing the importance of age-appropriate explanations to support adjustment and engagement with care.
